config.editorData:
ESA write path — the log, and the cost of keeping it tidy

ESA does not write in place. It appends to a log, acknowledges the write once it is logged, and later reclaims space by cleaning partially-used segments. That makes writes fast and makes housekeeping a first-class source of latency.

This screen exists because none of that work was visible anywhere in this pack. Worst case segment cleaning latency was measured at 370 milliseconds against a 1.3 millisecond average on an otherwise idle cluster.

Read it top down: the zDOM tables give the layer's own latency and throughput, the write path internals show how hard the metadata and caching machinery is working, and segment cleaning shows the reclamation cost. The log fill percentage is the leading indicator — as it rises, cleaning has to work harder and write amplification goes up with it.

One caveat, stated plainly. The zDOM maximum latency columns read in whole seconds, which is not credible as an interval maximum and is very likely a since-boot high-water mark that the Performance Service does not document as such. Use the average columns for decisions until that is confirmed.

zDOM - cluster

Renders the vSAN zDOM Cluster view.

Read Latency — Average read latency at this layer. Compare the same column across the client, owner and component manager views: the layer where the number first becomes large is the layer to investigate.

Write Latency — Average write latency at this layer. On ESA a write is acknowledged after it is logged, so this is usually far lower than the component manager's figure beneath it.

Read IOPS — Read operations per second. Always read beside latency: high latency at high IOPS is a busy VM, high latency at near-zero IOPS is a sick one.

Write IOPS — Write operations per second.

Read Throughput — Bytes per second read at this layer.

Write Throughput — Bytes per second written at this layer.

Outstanding IO — Outstanding IO: operations issued and not yet completed. Latency multiplied by nothing tells you why it is high -- this does. High latency with high outstanding IO is queueing, high latency with low outstanding IO is a slow device.

zDOM - per host

Renders the vSAN zDOM Per Host view.

Read Latency — Average read latency at this layer. Compare the same column across the client, owner and component manager views: the layer where the number first becomes large is the layer to investigate.

Write Latency — Average write latency at this layer. On ESA a write is acknowledged after it is logged, so this is usually far lower than the component manager's figure beneath it.

Read latency max us — Worst read latency recorded in the zDOM layer. Reads 9.7 seconds here, which is not credible as an interval maximum -- it is very likely a since-boot high-water mark that the Performance Service does not document as such. Treat a large value as unverified until the behaviour is confirmed, and use the average column for decisions.

Write latency max us — Worst write latency recorded in the zDOM layer. Subject to the same caveat as the read column beside it.

Unmap latency max us — Worst unmap latency recorded in the zDOM layer.

Read IOPS — Read operations per second. Always read beside latency: high latency at high IOPS is a busy VM, high latency at near-zero IOPS is a sick one.

Write IOPS — Write operations per second.

Read Throughput — Bytes per second read at this layer.

Write Throughput — Bytes per second written at this layer.

Outstanding IO — Outstanding IO: operations issued and not yet completed. Latency multiplied by nothing tells you why it is high -- this does. High latency with high outstanding IO is queueing, high latency with low outstanding IO is a slow device.

Outstanding IO (write) — Outstanding write operations.

Write path internals

Renders the vSAN zDOM Write Path view.

Disc used percent (max) — Highest proportion of the log structure in use. Measured at 32% here. As this climbs the segment cleaner has to work harder and write amplification rises, so it is a leading indicator for the latency columns on the segment cleaning view.

Latency avg total op IO — Average latency of all zDOM operations together.

Latency avg transaction bank — Average latency of transaction bank operations -- the in-memory staging area a write passes through before it is logged.

Cache ref (rate, total) — Rate of references to zDOM's metadata cache, all kinds together. Context for the breakdown columns beside it rather than a health signal.

Bank flush total cache ref (rate) — Cache references caused by flushing the transaction bank to disk.

Seg cleaning context data total cache ref (rate) — Cache references caused by segment cleaning. Rising here while guest IOPS is flat means housekeeping is taking a larger share of the metadata path.

Transaction prefetch total cache ref (rate) — Cache references from prefetching metadata ahead of need. Effective prefetch is why read latency stays low; this is the work behind that.

Transaction lookup cache ref (rate) — Cache references from metadata lookups that could not be satisfied by prefetch.

Transaction (read, write, rate) — Ratio of read to write transactions in the zDOM layer. Characterises the workload rather than its health.

Checkpoint worker wakeup ms — Interval at which the checkpoint worker wakes to persist metadata. Steady by design; a change means configuration changed or the worker is falling behind.

Segment cleaning

Renders the vSAN Segment Cleaning Per Host view.

IOPS seg cleaner unmap — Operations per second performed by the segment cleaner. ESA writes to a log and must later reclaim partially-used segments; this is that housekeeping, and it competes with guest IO for the same disks.

Latency avg seg cleaner unmap — Average latency of segment cleaning work.

Latency max seg cleaner unmap — Worst segment cleaning latency in the interval. Measured at 370 milliseconds here against a 1.3 millisecond average. Housekeeping stalling for a third of a second is worth knowing about, and no other screen in this pack would show it.

Latency standard deviation seg cleaner unmap — Spread of segment cleaning latency.

Throughput seg cleaner unmap — Bytes per second the segment cleaner is moving. This is write amplification made visible: capacity the disks are spending on vSAN's own bookkeeping rather than on guest data.

Seg cleaner unmap leaf owner max latency avg us — Worst average latency any single replica contributed to segment cleaning. Isolates one bad disk inside an otherwise healthy cleaning cycle.

Unmap IOPS — Space-reclamation operations per second, including those originated by guests trimming their filesystems.

Unmap Latency — Average latency of unmap operations.

Latency max unmap — Worst unmap latency in the interval.

Unmap count — Lifetime count of unmap operations. Cumulative since boot.

Back end - per host

Renders the vSAN Host DOM Component Manager view.

Read Latency — Average read latency at this layer. Compare the same column across the client, owner and component manager views: the layer where the number first becomes large is the layer to investigate.

Latency (max, read) — Worst read latency in the interval. Read beside the average: a large gap is a tail-latency problem, which guests feel as stalls even when the average looks fine.

Write Latency — Average write latency at this layer. On ESA a write is acknowledged after it is logged, so this is usually far lower than the component manager's figure beneath it.

Latency (max, write) — Worst write latency in the interval. Measured here at 14.9 ms against a 957 microsecond average -- a fifteenfold tail on an idle cluster, and the kind of thing an average hides completely.

Latency standard deviation (write) — Spread of write latency. High spread with a low average means the work is bimodal: most operations fast, some very slow.

Read IOPS — Read operations per second. Always read beside latency: high latency at high IOPS is a busy VM, high latency at near-zero IOPS is a sick one.

Write IOPS — Write operations per second.

Outstanding IO — Outstanding IO: operations issued and not yet completed. Latency multiplied by nothing tells you why it is high -- this does. High latency with high outstanding IO is queueing, high latency with low outstanding IO is a slow device.

Read Throughput — Bytes per second read at this layer.

Write Throughput — Bytes per second written at this layer.

VM disk queue depth (write) — Queue depth for writes to virtual disk objects at the component manager. Depth is the cause; the latency columns are the effect.

VM disk dispatched cost (write) — Accumulated cost of dispatched virtual disk writes, in vSAN's internal scheduling units. Not comparable to a time or a byte count -- useful for comparing hosts against each other, not against a threshold.

Namespace dispatched cost (write) — The same cost measure for namespace objects, which hold VM configuration rather than guest data. Large values here with small virtual disk values mean the work is metadata, not guest IO.
